doc.title: Rashied Ali and Henry Grimes interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, January 30, 2009

title: Duo interplay between bass and drums
summary: Ali and Grimes describe chasing each other's ideas and knowing when to end a long piece.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Great drummers: who they admired and why

blocks.x: When you guys work together, or this may happen in other combinations; I know you work with a lot of different people. If something, if you’re playing a song that is not preconceived, are there times when you’re playing together where you feel like we’re sort of just marking time here, waiting for something to gel?

Yeah, it’s true, but I think it’s more of a guess than accurate. You know, what’s going to be coming. But that’s a thought because when a lot of the rhetorics and pragmatics, there are a lot of guys playing, you know kind of do certain meaning in their playing and in others’ and it’s all happening at once. You know, that may not necessarily mean it as a sign of times to come, something that is, you know, that kind of a sign. It’s not really that way.
Rashied, how do you know when, like if I look on your CD here and there’s a song that’s twenty-some minutes long, is there something inside you guys that tells you this one’s over now?

Well we work on each other’s — we work with each other on things and we listen to each other and we kind of work off of each other, you know. You sort of just bounce off of each other. Like Henry would get into an idea of something and I would catch up to it sometimes, or sometimes I can’t, or maybe I’ll be struggling trying to deal with it. But not struggling to the point where you can notice it at all, just within myself. And then I say oh, here’s where it’s at. And I will get there and when I get there sometimes Henry would be going someplace else. All right? Now I’m after it again. It’s just that it’s like we are playing tag you know. I catch up and then it’s like wow, then I’m looking again and I catch up and then we come together with all this stuff and then we’ll be apart, then we’re together, then I’m after him then he’s after me. And it’s just like that. So it’s very exciting, I mean for the listener, but sometimes I’ll be hurting up there. But, at the same time, it’s a good hurt. It’s something that is challenging I would say, it’s very challenging.

Is there one of your hands or feet or one of your instruments that you find when you’re not really comfortable, and as you said you’re trying to find out where is it, whatever it is, do you find that you rely on something just to play more until you can really find it —

Well yeah, well you know I definitely have something that I can fall back on. You know I mean I have something that, I mean that’s my experience and my prowess and my experience, that I pull on everything when I’m playing just with Henry because I’m dealing with just the bass. You know I’m not dealing with horns and piano and all that. So I have to rely on my experience and prowess and so a lot of times I could get something, I could pull up on something that would get me through the mass, you know. It can get me through the uneasiness until I can catch up to what’s happening. Now I don’t stop, I just keep going until it comes into view and then I’m okay again. And that © Fillius Jazz Archive -18-

lasts until it changes again. So, because it’s always different, it’s always changing. And then we keep up some stuff for maybe 20 minutes or 25 minutes, and then after a while we’ll sort of look at each other and go okay, this is, it’s time to leave this now. And bang, we quit. You know what I mean?
